proposed_english: by the name that says / under the name
rationale: Compound preposition introducing a quoted divine saying that names/labels the subject. Built on ⲁ- ('to') + ⲡ- (article) + ⲡⲉⲛ (Lyc. for ⲣⲉⲛ 'name,' cf. glossary ϯⲡⲉⲛ 'to give a name'). Functions to mark the imperative 'sprout up as grass' as the naming-saying that determined the archons' first form. Likely echoes the creation-imperative tradition (cf. Gen 1:11).

Hapax in the corpus to date. Listed in line 2 alongside ⲥⲁⲣⲁⲣⲁⲩ 'brambles' as a class of bitter/thorny plants in the catalogue of vegetation molded from the enthumesis. Possibly Lyc. for ϣⲟⲛⲧⲉ/ϣⲟⲩⲏ 'thorn' or related thorn-bush term. Confidence low; flagged for parallels.

Reduplicated plural noun in catalogue of bitter plants (line 2). Etymology uncertain; possibly cognate with ⲥⲣ̄- 'thorn' family or with a tangling/scattering root (ⲥⲣ̄ⲣ̄ 'scatter'). Functions as the second member in a list of thorny undergrowth molded from the enthumesis.

Possibly Lyc. for ⲕⲏⲙⲉ/ⲕⲏⲙⲏ 'Egypt' (as 'black-land') or simply 'black, darkness.' In line 2 'thornbushes of ⲕⲉⲙ' likely names a dark/desolate locus characteristic of the bitter plants. Could alternatively be a plant-species name. Confidence low.

Compound: ⲟⲩⲁⲙ- ('eater of,' agentive of ⲟⲩⲱⲙ 'eat') + ⲥⲁⲣⲓ̄ ('flesh,' Lyc. for ⲥⲁⲣⲝ). Standard Coptic agentive formation. The 'flesh-eating archons' constitute one of two ranks of dark powers in this kephalaion's tree-typology — those whose enthumesis is sealed in inedible/fruitless trees. Distinct from the herbivorous powers whose enthumesis manifests in nourishing fruit-bearing trees.

Lyc. reflex of ⲉⲍⲉ/ⲉⲓⲱⲍⲉ 'ox, cattle.' Used in line 7-8 paired with ⲥⲁⲣⲓ̄ 'flesh' to designate the embodiment-state the powers had not yet attained when first planted as grass: 'they were not planted themselves as flesh and as ox.'

Per Crum 39a, ⲃⲟⲟⲛⲉ = 'fodder, hay' — animal feed. Used in line 13 in negated doublet ⲟⲩⲧⲉ ⲁⲧⲛⲁϩⲣⲉ ⲟⲩⲧⲉ ⲁⲧⲃⲟⲟⲛⲉ 'neither as food (for humans) nor as fodder (for animals)' — marking the inedible trees as serving no nutritional purpose for any creature.

Coptic action-noun: ⲧ- (article) + ϭⲓⲛ- ('the manner of, the act of') + ⲣⲱⲧ ('sprout, grow, take root'). The technical term for the present kephalaion's botanical-typological exposition: the various ways in which trees sprout, fail to sprout, or are propagated by cuttings.

Lyc. verb in line 26 governing cuttings cut from root. Possibly ⲡⲱⲣⲭ̄/ⲡⲱⲣϣ̄ 'separate, scatter, spread' with regular Lyc. ⲍ for ϫ/ϣ. Alternative reading 'wither' (ⲡⲱⲱⲣⲉ) is contextually weaker since the verb is followed by 'and they raise them again (and bear fruit).' Captures the scattering of cuttings into soil for propagation. Confidence low.

Hapax in line 24, in the phrase 'they bear fruit growing upward, ⲛⲩϩ̄ a tree of [its branches].' Possibly Lyc. ⲛⲏⲩ 'coming/being' (qualitative) or ⲛⲟⲩⲍⲏ 'themselves,' or a compound on ⲛⲁ-/ⲛⲏⲩ-. Functions as the verbal/adverbial element joining the upward growth to the formation of a new tree from cuttings. Confidence low.
Compound directional: ϩⲉⲓ ('fall, go') + ⲁⲍⲣⲏⲓ̈ ('upward'). Likely an idiomatic rising-verb where 'fall upward' = 'rise, grow up.' In line 24 describes the upward growth of fruit-producing cuttings.
